tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.

If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.

- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
schema.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

"""Lesson 11 — LLM evals for the prompts. Opt in:  pytest -m llm

An eval is a test whose subject is non-deterministic, so:
- each case is a GOLDEN input (an exact message, today's date, what's already stored) and a few
  checks written in code — the fields that must or must not appear, not an exact match;
- each case pins one rule from the prompt, and most came from a real failure or a review;
- run each case several times (EVAL_TRIALS=3 pytest -m llm ...) and look at the pass RATE.
  One pass proves little; a case that fails 1 run in 3 is a prompt bug, not noise.

These call extract_memories() directly: no database, just prompt in, Extraction out.
"""
import datetime as dt
import os
import re

import pytest

from companion.extract import extract_memories, summarize_episode

pytestmark = pytest.mark.llm
TRIALS = int(os.environ.get("EVAL_TRIALS", "1"))
WED = dt.date(2026, 11, 18)  # a Wednesday: "Friday" -> 2026-11-20


def extract(msg, reply="Got it.", candidates=(), entities=(), earlier=(), today=WED):
    return extract_memories("Riley", msg, reply, list(candidates), list(entities), today, list(earlier))


def trials(check):
    """Run a case TRIALS times; fail with every failing output if any trial fails."""
    failures = []
    for _ in range(TRIALS):
        try:
            check()
        except AssertionError as e:
            failures.append(str(e))
    assert not failures, f"{len(failures)}/{TRIALS} trials failed:\n" + "\n---\n".join(failures)


def kinds(ex):
    return [m.kind for m in ex.memories]


def test_describing_own_behaviour_is_not_a_boundary(llm_ready):
    def check():
        ex = extract("I never talk to my dad anymore since the fight.", "That sounds really hard.")
        assert "boundary" not in kinds(ex), ex.model_dump_json(exclude_defaults=True)
    trials(check)

content.text:
Yes, I think it's a good fit, as long as it's an optional add-on and doesn't replace what you already have.

**What you have now**
- **Evals** ([test_11_extraction_evals.py](tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py)) are golden inputs checked in code, run several times so you look at the pass rate. They're simple and readable, and they work as a CI gate. Keep them.
- **Tracing** is the hand-rolled `trace` list in [companion/graph.py:107](companion/graph.py:107), shown in the web UI (Lesson 18). It's good for teaching because it shows memory-specific things like what recall found and where it came from. But it only covers the companion graph, it disappears when the process ends, and it doesn't show the prompts, token counts or timing of each LLM call.

**What MLflow would add**
- **Deeper traces almost for free.** `mlflow.langchain.autolog()` captures every LangGraph node, LLM call, prompt, output, token count and latency as nested spans. `mlflow.openai.autolog()` covers the direct OpenAI calls in `extract.py`. Neo4j calls aren't captured automatically, so you'd put `@mlflow.trace` on recall and the write path, the parts that matter most for debugging memory.
- **Eval history.** Right now a pass rate is printed once and lost. If each eval run is logged to MLflow, tagged with the prompt version and model, you can compare runs side by side and see which change broke "describing your own behaviour is not a boundary."
- **Runs locally.** `mlflow server` with a SQLite backend, or a service in your existing `docker-compose.yml`. No account needed.

**How I'd adopt it**
1. Put tracing behind an environment variable (e.g. `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI`), so the course still runs with zero extra setup and `mlflow` is an optional dependency group.
2. Keep pytest as the pass/fail gate, and have a fixture log each eval case's results to MLflow when tracking is on. Code checks stay the source of truth; MLflow is where you look at them over time.
3. Keep the Lesson 18 trace for teaching. You could also attach the same recall details to the MLflow spans so both show the same thing.
4. This could make a good Lesson 21 on observability and evals.

**Alternatives worth knowing**
- **Arize Phoenix** is lighter and focused only on tracing (OpenTelemetry-native). It's a good choice if you mostly want traces.
- **Langfuse** is very good but heavy to self-host (Postgres plus ClickHouse).
- **LangSmith** fits LangGraph most naturally but runs in the cloud, so it isn't local.

MLflow wins here because you want traces and eval tracking in one local tool. One cost: MLflow's LLM-judge scorers make extra model calls, so I'd hold off on those until the code-based checks stop being enough.

"""Shared fixtures. Three kinds of test live in this folder:

    unit       pure Python, no database, no LLM            always run, milliseconds
    db         real Neo4j, writes rolled back or isolated  run by default, skipped if Neo4j is down
    llm        real LLM calls, graded by code              opt in:  pytest -m llm

Rules the fixtures enforce:
- A test never leaves data behind: Cypher writes go through `tx` (rolled back), memory tests
  use their own `pytest` user, wiped before and after.
- A test whose lesson you haven't done yet is SKIPPED with a reason, not failed.
"""
import os
import sys

import pytest

# vectors live apart from a remote model's, so this is safe even when your chats use
# EMBED_BASE_URL. TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1 runs them on the model in .env (the README's release
# check): thresholds come from the active profile, so the same tests hold on either model.
if not os.getenv("TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS"):

def driver():
    from neo4j import GraphDatabase

    yield drv

@pytest.fixture
def tx(driver):
    """A transaction that is ALWAYS rolled back: write freely, nothing persists."""
    with driver.session(database="neo4j") as session:
        t = session.begin_transaction()
        try:
            yield t
        finally:
            if t.closed() is False:
                t.rollback()


def rows(driver, query: str, **params) -> list[dict]:
    records, _, _ = driver.execute_query(query, **params)

    """Skip the test unless `query` returns a truthy first value (a lesson prerequisite)."""
    found = rows(driver, query, **params)

def trials(check):
    """Run an eval case EVAL_TRIALS times (default 1); fail with every failing output."""
    import os
    n = int(os.environ.get("EVAL_TRIALS", "1"))

def build_companion(store: MemoryStore, background: Background | None = None,
                    trace: list[dict] | None = None):
    """The companion graph. With `background`, memory extraction runs on that worker.

    With `trace` (a list), every turn appends a dict showing what memory did (Lesson 18):
    what recall found, the exact system prompt, timings, and what extraction decided.
    The nodes fill it in as they run; a background job adds its part when it finishes."""
    llm = chat_model()
    to_redact: list[str] = []  # names forgotten by a background job, scrubbed on the next turn

    def turn() -> dict:
        return trace[-1] if trace else {}

    def recall(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        query = state["messages"][-1].content
        started = time.perf_counter()
        found = store.recall(query, today=_today(config))
        if trace is not None:
            trace.append({"n": len(trace) + 1, "message": query, "recall": found,
                          "recall_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000)})
        update = {"memory_context": format_context(found, _today(config))}
        if to_redact:
            terms = [to_redact.pop() for _ in range(len(to_redact))]
            update["messages"] = _redact(state["messages"], terms)
        return update

    def respond(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        today = _today(config)
        system = SystemMessage(PERSONA.format(
            name=store.agent, role=ROLES.get(store.agent, DEFAULT_ROLE), user=store.user_name,
            today=clock.describe(clock.now_for(today)),
            memory=state["memory_context"],
        ))
        recent = state["messages"][-RECENT_TURNS:]
        while recent and not isinstance(recent[0], HumanMessage):  # start the window on a user turn
            recent = recent[1:]
        started = time.perf_counter()
        reply = llm.invoke([system, *recent])
        if trace is not None:
            turn().update(system_prompt=system.content, window=len(recent),
                          history=len(state["messages"]),
                          respond_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000),
                          usage=getattr(reply, "usage_metadata", None))
        return {"messages": [reply]}

    def log(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        episode_id = config["configurable"]["thread_id"]
        store.log_turn(episode_id, store.user_name, state["messages"][-2].content)
        store.log_turn(episode_id, store.agent, state["messages"][-1].content)
        return {"memory_log": []}

        *_, asked, user_msg, _reply = [None, *state["messages"]]
        question = getattr(asked, "content", "") or ""
        if worth_remembering(user_msg.content, question):
            return "remember"
        if trace is not None:
            turn()["extraction"] = {"status": "skipped", "reason": "small talk: nothing to remember"}

            seen["extraction"] = {"status": "queued" if background is not None else "running",

        def job() -> list[str]:
            started = time.perf_counter()

            # what the previous one wrote.
            candidates = store.extraction_candidates(window, today=today)
            entities = store.known_entities()
            if trace is not None:
                seen["extraction"].update(status="running", waited_ms=round(
                    (time.time() - seen["extraction"]["queued_at"]) * 1000), candidates=candidates,
                    entities=entities)
            try:
                extraction = extract_memories(
                    store.user_name, said, answered, candidates=candidates, entities=entities,
                    today=today, earlier=earlier, companion=store.agent,
                )
                if os.environ.get("COMPANION_DEBUG_EXTRACT"):  # print the raw LLM extraction

                llm_done = time.perf_counter()
                log = store.apply(extraction, episode_id, today)
            except Exception as e:

                raise

                    llm_ms=round((llm_done - started) * 1000),
                    write_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - llm_done) * 1000))

def build_companion(store: MemoryStore, background: Background | None = None,
                    trace: list[dict] | None = None):
    """The companion graph. With `background`, memory extraction runs on that worker.

    With `trace` (a list), every turn appends a dict showing what memory did (Lesson 18):
    what recall found, the exact system prompt, timings, and what extraction decided.
    The nodes fill it in as they run; a background job adds its part when it finishes."""
    llm = chat_model()
    to_redact: list[str] = []  # names forgotten by a background job, scrubbed on the next turn

    def turn() -> dict:
        return trace[-1] if trace else {}

    def recall(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        query = state["messages"][-1].content
        started = time.perf_counter()
        found = store.recall(query, today=_today(config))
        if trace is not None:
            trace.append({"n": len(trace) + 1, "message": query, "recall": found,
                          "recall_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000)})
        update = {"memory_context": format_context(found, _today(config))}
        if to_redact:
            terms = [to_redact.pop() for _ in range(len(to_redact))]
            update["messages"] = _redact(state["messages"], terms)
        return update

    def respond(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        today = _today(config)
        system = SystemMessage(PERSONA.format(
            name=store.agent, role=ROLES.get(store.agent, DEFAULT_ROLE), user=store.user_name,
            today=clock.describe(clock.now_for(today)),
            memory=state["memory_context"],
        ))
        recent = state["messages"][-RECENT_TURNS:]
        while recent and not isinstance(recent[0], HumanMessage):  # start the window on a user turn
            recent = recent[1:]
        started = time.perf_counter()
        reply = llm.invoke([system, *recent])
        if trace is not None:
            turn().update(system_prompt=system.content, window=len(recent),
                          history=len(state["messages"]),
                          respond_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000),
                          usage=getattr(reply, "usage_metadata", None))
        return {"messages": [reply]}

    def log(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        episode_id = config["configurable"]["thread_id"]
        store.log_turn(episode_id, store.user_name, state["messages"][-2].content)
        store.log_turn(episode_id, store.agent, state["messages"][-1].content)
        return {"memory_log": []}

    def route(state: CompanionState) -> str:
        *_, asked, user_msg, _reply = [None, *state["messages"]]
        question = getattr(asked, "content", "") or ""
        if worth_remembering(user_msg.content, question):
            return "remember"
        if trace is not None:
            turn()["extraction"] = {"status": "skipped", "reason": "small talk: nothing to remember"}
        return END

    def remember(state: CompanionState, config: RunnableConfig):
        episode_id, today = config["configurable"]["thread_id"], _today(config)
        *before, user_msg, reply = state["messages"]
        earlier = [(store.user_name if isinstance(m, HumanMessage) else store.agent, m.content)
                   for m in before]  # extract_memories marks the companion's lines as non-sources
        window = " ".join(text for _, text in earlier[-2:]) + " " + user_msg.content
        said, answered = user_msg.content, reply.content
        seen = turn()
        if trace is not None:
            seen["extraction"] = {"status": "queued" if background is not None else "running",
                                  "queued_at": time.time()}

        def job() -> list[str]:
            started = time.perf_counter()
            # Candidates are read INSIDE the job: queued jobs run in order, so this one sees
            # what the previous one wrote.
            candidates = store.extraction_candidates(window, today=today)
            entities = store.known_entities()
            if trace is not None:
                seen["extraction"].update(status="running", waited_ms=round(
                    (time.time() - seen["extraction"]["queued_at"]) * 1000), candidates=candidates,
                    entities=entities)
            try:
                extraction = extract_memories(
                    store.user_name, said, answered, candidates=candidates, entities=entities,
                    today=today, earlier=earlier, companion=store.agent,
                )
                if os.environ.get("COMPANION_DEBUG_EXTRACT"):  # print the raw LLM extraction
                    print("     raw extraction:", extraction.model_dump_json(exclude_defaults=True))
                llm_done = time.perf_counter()
                log = store.apply(extraction, episode_id, today)
            except Exception as e:
                if trace is not None:
                    seen["extraction"].update(status="failed", error=f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                raise
            to_redact.extend(store.forgotten_terms)
            if trace is not None:
                seen["extraction"].update(
                    status="done", extracted=extraction.model_dump(exclude_defaults=True), log=log,
                    llm_ms=round((llm_done - started) * 1000),
                    write_ms=round((time.perf_counter() - llm_done) * 1000))
            return log

        if background is not None:
            background.submit(job)
            return {"memory_log": []}
        update = {"memory_log": job()}
        if to_redact:  # also scrub the live conversation, or the next turn re-learns it
            terms = [to_redact.pop() for _ in range(len(to_redact))]
            update["messages"] = _redact(state["messages"], terms)

Covers framework autologging, custom spans, backend setup, and persisted trace verification. --- # Instrument MLflow tracing Reuse working tracing for investigation or evaluation. ## Prerequisites - Check entry point, language/framework, SDK version, tracking URI, experiment, and deployment identity. - Preserve destinations and providers. Explicit application destinations override inherited environment values; assistant telemetry may use another experiment. - Read [Python](references/python.md) or [TypeScript](references/typescript.md) for the runtime. ## Step 1: Check the destination (Databricks only) For OSS or SageMaker, keep the configured backend and proceed to Step 2. - Read [UC setup](references/databricks.md) **before editing**; validate auth/workspace. - Reuse the explicit destination; otherwise resolve schema choice before provisioning. - Discover an accessible warehouse automatically. Default to UC; legacy storage requires an explicit request. ## Step 2: Enable framework tracing - Enable the matching integration before execution. LangGraph uses `mlflow.langchain.autolog()`, not `mlflow.langgraph.autolog()`. - Do not wrap automatically traced nodes, tools, or models again. Reserve manual spans for uncaptured work or an outer application boundary. ## Step 3: Capture application work - Trace meaningful root, LLM, retrieval, tool, routing, and external I/O (files/queues). Skip utility, configuration, and logging noise. - Capture actual relevant inputs/outputs explicitly for manual spans; redact before export. ## Step 4: Run one request - Run one representative request; record start/end epoch milliseconds. - Save its trace ID immediately in-process: `mlflow.get_last_active_trace_id()` in Python; the active span's ID in TypeScript. - Write/flush the trace ID to a file or captured stdout before readback; retain it if the process is cancelled. Do not rerun to recover an ID. ## Verification - Fetch a **persisted application trace**, not a local span or old trace. - Set a **60-second wall-clock process deadline** for readback, including flush, SDK retries, requests, and backoff. Terminate at expiry unless the user explicitly requests deeper troubleshooting. - Tool yields/thread-wait timeouts do not cancel calls. Without cancellation, report backend verification as unperformed. - Flush once (`mlflow.flush_trace_async_logging()` / `await mlflow.flushTraces()`); fetch the saved ID. - Without an ID, search once in the configured experiment with run-time bounds, `max_results=1`, and spans included. - Every UC search needs `trace.timestamp_ms`; result limits do not bound scans. Python `search_traces()` has no `start_time` keyword. For Python readback, adapt this recipe to the saved run values and enforce the deadline externally: ```python mlflow.flush_trace_async_logging() if trace_id: trace = mlflow.get_trace(trace_id) else: traces = mlflow.search_traces( locations=[experiment_id], filter_string=(f"trace.timestamp_ms >= {run_start_ms} " f"AND trace.timestamp_ms <= {run_end_ms}"), max_results=1, return_type="list", include_spans=True, ) trace = traces[0] if traces else None assert trace is not None, "No persisted trace read back" assert run_start_ms <= trace.info.request_time <= run_end_ms assert trace.data.spans, "No spans captured" ``` - Inspect expected root/graph, model, retrieval, and tool spans and actual I/O. Confirm the application's request, not scorer or assistant telemetry. - Check experiment/location from returned metadata, or the bound UC location if no experiment ID exists. - Reuse returned spans; stop after success. - Retry at most once after a concrete quick fix **within the original budget**. - Stop on missing provider keys, auth/permission errors, warehouse timeouts, or `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`/429. - No parallel searches, repeated agent runs, direct UC SQL, raw REST, alternate credentials, or warehouse fallbacks. - Report operation/error, captured ID, successes, and unverified results. Request the missing prerequisite, not secrets. - Keep instrumentation changes if backend verification is blocked; pause evaluation until tracing is verified. Return the verified trace ID/link and observed spans. For Databricks use the [verified trace URL rules](references/databricks.md#link-to-the-verified-trace), not an experiment-only link. Do not label an unverified link as proof. ## References - Deployment, async export, sampling: [production](references/production.md). - Async/thread context, redaction, caught errors or links: [advanced patterns](references/advanced-patterns.md). - Cross-service parent propagation: [distributed tracing](references/distributed-tracing.md). - User ratings tied to traces: [feedback collection](references/feedback-collection.md). - Unreadable non-chat root previews: [root span previews](references/root-span-previews.md). - Explaining captured behavior: `mlflow-trace-analysis`; implementing a requested behavior fix: `mlflow-agent-improvement`, carrying the trace evidence. These are optional follow-on tasks. - Other integrations: [automatic tracing docs](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/app-instrumentation/automatic.md). Check installed signatures/types. - Missing/moved topic: [llms.txt](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/llms.txt). Docs unavailable: use local recipes and installed API introspection; stop if correctness remains uncertain.

# Python tracing

## Setup and integration choice

Reuse `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` and `MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_ID` or existing application configuration. Install only if needed (for example, `pip install 'mlflow>=3.8.0'`). For Databricks, follow [UC setup](databricks.md), including its newer version requirement and absolute workspace experiment path; setting the tracking URI alone is insufficient.

For an unconfigured OSS destination, set the chosen server and experiment; keep any supplied configuration:

```python
import mlflow
mlflow.set_tracking_uri(tracking_uri)  # Only if not already configured
mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_id=experiment_id)
```

To create an experiment by name, use `mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_name=experiment_name)`.

Choose the framework already in use:

```python
import mlflow
mlflow.langchain.autolog()  # LangChain and LangGraph, before application execution
```

LangGraph has no `mlflow.langgraph.autolog()`. Its graph, nodes, tools and model calls are autologged: do not decorate them again. Use the matching integration for other frameworks, such as `mlflow.openai.autolog()` for the OpenAI SDK. Do not enable unrelated integrations. See [automatic tracing](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/app-instrumentation/automatic.md) for framework/version details.

## Custom application work

Prefer a decorator, which captures arguments and return values. A deliberate outer application span may group custom work with autologged calls.

```python
from mlflow.entities import SpanType

@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER)
def retrieve_documents(query):
    return search_index(query)  # Adapt to the existing application
```

Use `mlflow.start_span()` for dynamic names or code without a function boundary. Set both inputs and outputs explicitly:

```python
with mlflow.start_span(name="retrieve_documents", span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER) as span:
    span.set_inputs({"query": query})
    result = search_index(query)
    span.set_outputs(result)
```

Record actual retrieved documents, messages and tool results, not just counts. Apply privacy policy before export; any content reduction should be deliberate and documented. Explicit `span.set_inputs()` / `set_outputs()` override automatic capture. For compact root values versus display-only changes, read [root previews](root-span-previews.md).

With autologging enabled, decorate the custom entry point with `@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.CHAIN)` to group its retrieval and autologged model calls in one trace; do not redecorate the model calls.

RAG wiring: [complete retrieval-to-prompt example](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/llm-judge/rag.md#complete-rag-example).

## Session metadata and attributes

Inside the active application span, attach the real user's/session's identifiers; do not collapse unrelated conversations under a shared default session:

```python
mlflow.update_current_trace(user=user_id, session_id=session_id)
span = mlflow.get_current_active_span()
if span:
    span.set_attribute("description", "Retrieve account records")
```

For an autologged LangGraph node, setting an attribute on its existing active span is sufficient; a new decorator is unnecessary. Use a node docstring as a description only when useful.

## Verify and extend

Follow [persisted readback](../SKILL.md#verification), including saving `mlflow.get_last_active_trace_id()` immediately after the run in the same process. Missing traces require checking the existing destination, experiment, autolog warnings and auth before changing instrumentation.

- Threads, async, redaction or handled exceptions: [advanced patterns](advanced-patterns.md).
- Other manual API options: [manual tracing](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/app-instrumentation/manual-tracing.md), checked against the installed version.

"""Lesson 14 — run memory extraction in the background, so replies never wait for it.

Extraction is an extra LLM call plus graph writes: one to several seconds per message. The
reply doesn't need it, so the chat hands the job to a worker and answers straight away.

One worker THREAD per conversation, not a pool:
- jobs for the same user run in order. Job 2's prompt includes the memories job 1 wrote
  ("you already know Maya is the sister"), so they must not overlap.
- MemoryStore._write() also locks the user's node, so even writers in other processes (a
  web server with several workers, a nightly job) can't interleave. The queue is for order
  and latency, the lock is for correctness.

Results come back as log lines: `drain()` returns what's finished without blocking (the chat
prints them before the next prompt), `wait()` blocks until the queue is empty (call it before
the end-of-episode pass, which must see every memory).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import queue
import threading
import traceback
from concurrent.futures import Future, ThreadPoolExecutor


class Background:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1, thread_name_prefix="memory")
        self._pending: list[Future] = []
        self._done: queue.SimpleQueue[str] = queue.SimpleQueue()
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def submit(self, job) -> Future:
        """Queue `job()` (returns a list of log lines). Returns at once."""
        def run():
            try:
                lines = job() or []
            except Exception as e:  # a background error must surface somewhere
                traceback.print_exc()
                lines = [f"memory update failed: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"]
            for line in lines:
                self._done.put(line)

        with self._lock:
            future = self._pool.submit(run)
            self._pending.append(future)
        return future

    def drain(self) -> list[str]:
        """Log lines from jobs that have finished so far. Never blocks."""
        lines = []
        while True:
            try:
                lines.append(self._done.get_nowait())
            except queue.Empty:
                return lines

    def wait(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> list[str]:
        """Block until every queued job has finished, then return their log lines."""
        with self._lock:
            pending, self._pending = self._pending, []
        for future in pending:
            future.result(timeout)
        return self.drain()

    @property
    def busy(self) -> bool:
        with self._lock:
            return any(not f.done() for f in self._pending)

    @property
    def queued(self) -> int:
        """Jobs submitted but not finished (the one running included)."""
        with self._lock:
            return sum(not f.done() for f in self._pending)

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._pool.shutdown(wait=True)

"""Lesson 14 — run memory extraction in the background, so replies never wait for it.

Extraction is an extra LLM call plus graph writes: one to several seconds per message. The
reply doesn't need it, so the chat hands the job to a worker and answers straight away.

One worker THREAD per conversation, not a pool:
- jobs for the same user run in order. Job 2's prompt includes the memories job 1 wrote
  ("you already know Maya is the sister"), so they must not overlap.
- MemoryStore._write() also locks the user's node, so even writers in other processes (a
  web server with several workers, a nightly job) can't interleave. The queue is for order
  and latency, the lock is for correctness.

Results come back as log lines: `drain()` returns what's finished without blocking (the chat
prints them before the next prompt), `wait()` blocks until the queue is empty (call it before
the end-of-episode pass, which must see every memory).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import queue
import threading
import traceback
from concurrent.futures import Future, ThreadPoolExecutor


class Background:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1, thread_name_prefix="memory")
        self._pending: list[Future] = []
        self._done: queue.SimpleQueue[str] = queue.SimpleQueue()
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def submit(self, job) -> Future:
        """Queue `job()` (returns a list of log lines). Returns at once."""
        def run():
            try:
                lines = job() or []
            except Exception as e:  # a background error must surface somewhere
                traceback.print_exc()
                lines = [f"memory update failed: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"]
            for line in lines:
                self._done.put(line)

        with self._lock:
            future = self._pool.submit(run)
            self._pending.append(future)
        return future

    def drain(self) -> list[str]:
        """Log lines from jobs that have finished so far. Never blocks."""
        lines = []
        while True:
            try:
                lines.append(self._done.get_nowait())
            except queue.Empty:
                return lines

    def wait(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> list[str]:
        """Block until every queued job has finished, then return their log lines."""
        with self._lock:
            pending, self._pending = self._pending, []
        for future in pending:
            future.result(timeout)
        return self.drain()

    @property
    def busy(self) -> bool:
        with self._lock:
            return any(not f.done() for f in self._pending)

    @property
    def queued(self) -> int:
        """Jobs submitted but not finished (the one running included)."""
        with self._lock:
            return sum(not f.done() for f in self._pending)

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._pool.shutdown(wait=True)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- MLflow eval logging (optional)
# With MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI set (observability.py), `pytest -m llm` becomes one MLflow run:
#   params   the models, EVAL_TRIALS and a hash of the prompts, so runs can be compared;
#   metrics  passed / failed / pass_rate;
#   evals.json  one row per case: outcome, duration, the failure, and its trace id;
#   traces   each case is one trace holding every LLM call its trials made.
# The pass/fail verdict is still pytest's; MLflow is where you compare runs and read the prompts.
import observability  # noqa: E402

_eval_rows: list[dict] = []


def _start_eval_run():
    import hashlib
    import subprocess

    import mlflow

    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
    prompts = hashlib.sha256()
    for f in ("companion/extract.py", "companion/graph.py"):  # where the prompts live
        prompts.update((root / f).read_bytes())
    sha = subprocess.run(["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"], cwd=root,
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    dirty = subprocess.run(["git", "status", "--porcelain"], cwd=root,
                           capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"evals {sha}{'+dirty' if dirty else ''}")
    mlflow.log_params({
        "llm_model": config.LLM_MODEL, "extraction_model": config.LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL,
        "embed_model": config.EMBED_MODEL, "eval_trials": os.environ.get("EVAL_TRIALS", "1"),
        "prompts_sha": prompts.hexdigest()[:12], "git_sha": sha, "git_dirty": bool(dirty),
    })


@pytest.hookimpl(hookwrapper=True)
def pytest_runtest_call(item):
    """Each LLM eval case runs inside one span, so all its trials' LLM calls form one trace."""
    if not (observability.enabled() and item.get_closest_marker("llm")):
        yield
        return
    import mlflow

    if mlflow.active_run() is None:
        _start_eval_run()
    with observability.span(item.nodeid.split("::")[-1], "CHAIN",
                            inputs={"test": item.nodeid}) as sp:
        observability.tag_trace(eval_case=item.nodeid)
        item.stash[_trace_key] = sp.trace_id
        outcome = yield
        if outcome.excinfo:
            sp.set_outputs({"failed": str(outcome.excinfo[1])[:4000]})


_trace_key = pytest.StashKey[str]()


@pytest.hookimpl(hookwrapper=True)
def pytest_runtest_makereport(item, call):
    outcome = yield
    report = outcome.get_result()
    if not (observability.enabled() and item.get_closest_marker("llm")):
        return
    if report.when == "call" or (report.when == "setup" and report.skipped):
        _eval_rows.append({
            "case": item.nodeid, "outcome": report.outcome,
            "seconds": round(report.duration, 2),
            "failure": str(report.longrepr)[-4000:] if report.failed else "",
            "trace_id": item.stash.get(_trace_key, ""),
        })


def pytest_sessionfinish(session):
    if not (observability.enabled() and _eval_rows):
        return
    import mlflow

    if mlflow.active_run() is None:  # every case was skipped before it ran
        return
    passed = sum(r["outcome"] == "passed" for r in _eval_rows)
    failed = sum(r["outcome"] == "failed" for r in _eval_rows)
    mlflow.log_metrics({"passed": passed, "failed": failed,
                        "pass_rate": passed / (passed + failed) if passed + failed else 0.0})
    mlflow.log_table({k: [r[k] for r in _eval_rows] for k in _eval_rows[0]}, "evals.json")
    mlflow.end_run("FAILED" if failed else "FINISHED")
EOF

## Tests and evals

Every lesson has tests in [`tests/`](tests), named after it (`test_05_vectors_and_graphrag.py`).

```bash
uv run python -m pytest                    # unit + database tests: seconds, free (default)
uv run python -m pytest -m "not db and not llm"   # unit tests only, no Neo4j needed
uv run python -m pytest -m llm             # LLM evals: real calls, cost money
EVAL_TRIALS=3 uv run python -m pytest -m llm tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py   # pass rates
```

A `-m` on the command line *replaces* the default `-m "not llm"` in `pytest.ini`, so spell
out `and not llm` when you add your own filter. Database tests never leave data behind: writes run in rolled-back transactions, and memory
tests use their own `pytest` user. A test for a lesson you haven't done yet is skipped with a
reason. [Lesson 0](lessons/00-setup.md#test-it) explains the three kinds of test, and each
lesson ends with a *Test it* section on what its tests teach.

### Release check: on the model you ship

The default run pins the local embedding model, so it stays fast, free and offline. Before you
rely on a change, run the tests, the LLM evals and the scenarios on the model in your `.env`:

```bash
TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1 uv run python -m pytest              # ~5 min: every embedding is remote
TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1 uv run python -m pytest -m llm       # LLM evals, costs money
uv run python -m companion.scenarios                          # scripted conversations (use .env)
uv run python -m companion.calibrate                          # are the thresholds still right?
```

Tests that check a threshold read it from the active model's profile. Tests that are about one
model (bge-small's cross-encoder labels, a calibration pair a model is known to miss) say so
and check the right thing for each. A model's known misses are listed in
[`tests/test_19_embeddings.py`](tests/test_19_embeddings.py) (`KNOWN_MISSES`): anything else
failing is a regression.

|---|---|
| `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` | Neo4j 5.26 with APOC + GDS, data in named volumes |
| `.env.example` → `.env` | Neo4j credentials and LLM keys (`.env` is git-ignored) |
| `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `.python-version` | Dependencies, the exact tested versions, the Python version (`uv sync`) |
| `requirements.txt` | The same pinned versions for pip, generated from `uv.lock` |
| `config.py` | Loads `.env` for the scripts |
| `seed/00_seed.cypher` | Starting graph for Lesson 1 |
| `team_graph.py` | Lesson 4 — Python driver patterns |
| `embed.py` | Lesson 5 — local embeddings + vector index |
| `graphrag.py` | Lesson 5 — GraphRAG retrieval (+ LLM answer via the OpenAI SDK if `LLM_*` is set) |
| `team_agent.py` | Lesson 7 — LangGraph agent with graph tools |
| `companion/` | Lessons 8–10 — memory schema, store, extraction, LangGraph companion, CLI, demo |
| `companion/scenarios.py` | Lessons 11–12 — multi-session scenario tests for memory |
| `companion/ontology.py` | Lesson 12 — relation-type ontology: vocabulary, rules, inference |
| `companion/clock.py`, `companion/decay.py` | Lesson 13 — one clock; the forgetting curve |
| `companion/worker.py` | Lesson 14 — background extraction worker |
| `companion/insights.py` | Lesson 15 — graph embeddings (FastRP + kNN) and node similarity |
| `companion/web.py`, `companion/static/` | Lessons 17–18 — web UI (FastAPI + one HTML page) and the per-turn memory trace |
| `companion/embeddings.py`, `calibrate.py`, `reembed.py` | Lesson 19 — local or remote embeddings, per-model thresholds, measuring them, backfilling vectors |
| `companion/reextract.py` | Lesson 20 — re-read stored conversations under the current extraction rules |
| `docs/architecture.md` | Architecture diagrams (Mermaid) for lessons 7–17 (the *how*; design-decisions.md is the *why*) |
| `tests/`, `pytest.ini` | Per-lesson tests and LLM evals (see *Tests and evals*) |
| `docs/glossary.md` | Glossary of overlapping memory / graph / ontology terms, with a section per overloaded word |
| `docs/design-decisions.md` | Design decisions and tradeoffs, alternatives, gaps, comparison with other memory systems |
| `lessons/outputs/` | Recorded runs for lessons 7, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 17 |

def edit(p, a, b):

edit('README.md', """### Release check: on the model you ship""", """### Traces and eval history in MLflow (optional)

The Lesson 18 trace shows what memory did on one turn. For more detail, such as every LLM call
with its prompt, tokens and latency, plus eval runs you can compare over time, turn on local
MLflow tracing. It's off unless `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` is set:

```bash
uv sync --group observability                                    # once: installs mlflow
uv run --group observability mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --port 5001
```

Then, in another terminal, add `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://localhost:5001` to `.env` (or
prefix one command with it), and run as usual with `--group observability`:

```bash
uv run --group observability python -m companion                 # every turn is a trace
uv run --group observability python -m pytest -m llm             # one MLflow run per eval session
```

Open http://localhost:5001, experiment `companion`:
- **Traces**: a chat turn is one trace (`recall` → `respond` → `remember`, the LLM calls, and
  the Neo4j spans `store.recall`, `store.extraction_candidates`, `store.apply`), grouped by
  session. Background extraction is its own trace in the same session. An eval case is one
  trace holding every LLM call its trials made.
- **Runs**: each `pytest -m llm` session logs the models, `EVAL_TRIALS`, a hash of the prompt
  files, `passed`/`failed`/`pass_rate`, and an `evals.json` table with each case's failure
  and trace id. Compare runs to see which prompt or model change broke a case.

pytest still decides pass or fail; MLflow keeps the history. [`observability.py`](observability.py)
does the setup, and the hooks are at the end of [`tests/conftest.py`](tests/conftest.py).

### Release check: on the model you ship""")

""")

edit('observability.py', """    uv sync --group observability                              # once: installs mlflow

""", """    uv sync --group observability                         # once: installs mlflow

""")
EOF

content.text:
The MLflow prototype works on the `mlflow-tracing` branch: chat turns and eval runs both show up in a local MLflow server. It's off unless `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` is set, so the course runs as before without it. Nothing is committed yet.

**What it records once it's on**
- **A chat turn is one trace**, labelled with its session and user. Inside it you see recall → respond → remember, each LLM call with its prompt, output and tokens, and three Neo4j steps MLflow can't see by itself: `store.recall`, `store.extraction_candidates` and `store.apply`. I added those with a small decorator.
- **Background memory extraction is a separate trace** in the same session. By the time the background job runs, the turn's trace has already closed, so the two can't be one trace.
- **Each `pytest -m llm` session becomes one MLflow run.** It records the models, `EVAL_TRIALS`, a hash of the prompt files and the git commit, plus `passed`/`failed`/`pass_rate` and an `evals.json` table with each case's failure and trace ID. Each eval case is one trace holding every LLM call its trials made, linked to the run.

**What I checked**
- **Tracing off:** the normal test run gives the same results as `main`. Both have the same 13 failures, which come from the Lesson 1 seed data not being loaded in your database.
- **Tracing on:** I ran 3 boundary evals and read them back from the server. They appear as one run with 3 linked traces and a 100% pass rate.
- **A real chat turn:** I sent one message under a throwaway user, deleted afterwards. Both traces were saved with the right session and user, and the Neo4j spans showed real inputs.
- **Not checked:** the web UI and the terminal chat CLI. They use the same graph code, so they should behave the same.

**Files**
- [observability.py](observability.py) is new and does the setup. [config.py](config.py) turns it on.
- [companion/store.py](companion/store.py) and [companion/graph.py](companion/graph.py) have the Neo4j spans and session labels.
- The pytest hooks are at the end of [tests/conftest.py](tests/conftest.py).
- [README.md](README.md) has a new "Traces and eval history in MLflow" section. I also updated `.env.example` and `.gitignore`, and added the optional `observability` dependency group (MLflow 3.18).

**Things to know**
- MLflow is a large install, which is why it's an optional group and `requirements.txt` doesn't include it.
- I ran MLflow with `uv run` instead of adding a Docker service, to avoid pinning an image tag I couldn't check.
- Traces record full prompts and memory text, including anything sensitive. That's fine for a local server, but it would need masking before you send traces anywhere shared.

The MLflow server I started is still running at http://localhost:5001, so you can look around the experiment called `companion`. Stop it when you're done.

content.text:
I'd go partway: do more of the round trip in MLflow, but keep pytest as the place evals are defined and decided.

**Why not move the evals fully into MLflow (`mlflow.genai.evaluate`, its datasets and scorers)**
- Your eval checks are already plain code: "`boundary` must not appear in the kinds." Rewriting them as MLflow scorers would make them harder to read without making them more rigorous.
- MLflow would stop being optional. Today the course runs fully without it, and Lesson 11 teaches evals as pytest tests. Keeping that is worth more than having one framework for everything.
- pytest's skips, markers and CI exit codes already do the gating job well.

**What's worth adding: the round trip**
1. **Show each case's result on its trace.** Right now pass/fail lives in the run's `evals.json` table. Recording it on each trace (MLflow's `log_feedback`, with the failure as the reason) puts the verdict next to the exact prompt and output. You can then filter to failed traces and compare two runs case by case in MLflow's evaluation view. This is a small change inside the existing conftest hooks.
2. **Turn a bad chat trace into an eval case.** This is the real benefit of the round trip. You spot a wrong memory in a chat trace, a script reads that trace and writes a ready-to-edit pytest case from the message, the candidates and the known entities. You fill in the check, the case fails, you fix the prompt, and the next run shows the pass rate go up. That's how most of your current cases came about ("most came from a real failure or a review"); this just makes it faster.
3. **Log `companion.scenarios` runs the same way**, so the multi-session scenario checks get history too.

**When to go further into MLflow evaluation**
Do it once you want to check things code can't, like whether a reply actually used the recalled memory, or whether it respected a boundary in tone and not just in exact words. MLflow's LLM-judge scorers and evaluation datasets fit that well. I'd add them later as their own category, run against saved chat traces, alongside the code checks rather than replacing them.

content.content:
def _run(system: str, content: str) -> Extraction:
    llm = chat_model(LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL, temperature=0)
    try:
        return _structured(llm, Extraction, [SystemMessage(system), HumanMessage(content)])
    except Exception as e:  # never let memory extraction break the conversation
        print(f"  (memory extraction failed: {type(e).__name__}: {e})")
        return Extraction()


# Phrases that almost always set a boundary. Used as a tripwire, not as the extractor.
BOUNDARY_HINT = re.compile(
    r"\b(don'?t|do not|never|stop|please don'?t)\b.{0,25}\b(bring|mention|talk|ask|raise|remind)"
    r"|\bdon'?t want to (talk|hear|discuss)"
    r"|\b(rather|let'?s) not (talk|discuss|get into|go into)"
    r"|\bleave .{1,25} out of (it|this)", re.I)


def line(user: str, who: str, text: str) -> str:
    """One transcript line. The companion's lines are marked as non-sources (anti-echo)."""
    return f"{who}: {text}" if who == user else f"({who}, context only — not a source) {text}"


def extract_memories(user: str, user_msg: str, assistant_msg: str, candidates: list[dict],
                     entities: list[str], today: dt.date | None = None,
                     earlier: list[tuple[str, str]] = (), companion: str = COMPANION_NAME) -> Extraction:
    """Per-turn pass. `earlier` = (speaker, text) pairs before the latest exchange.

    Boundaries are safety-critical, so a regex tripwire double-checks the LLM: if the message
    looks like a boundary and none was extracted, extract once more with an explicit hint."""
    today = today or dt.date.today()
    context = "\n".join(line(user, who, text) for who, text in earlier[-CONTEXT_TURNS:])
    content = (f"Earlier in this conversation:\n{context}\n\n" if context else "") + \
              f"LATEST EXCHANGE:\n{user}: <message>{user_msg}</message>\n" + \
              line(user, companion, assistant_msg)
    system = _system(TURN_SYSTEM, user, candidates, entities, today)
    ex = _run(system, content)
